item.title: LAI #150: Can a Sandbox Stop a Hostile Agent?
item.guid: title:lai 150 can a sandbox stop a hostile agent
item.description: All five sandboxes blocked the attack. None protected the keys you handed the agent. Good morning, AI enthusiasts! An agent that can run for hours, remember past work, call tools, use credentials, and accept new instructions is useful for the same reasons it is hard to control. You have to decide what it can access, what it should remember, who is allowed to redirect it, which actions need approval, and what happens when something fails halfway through. Those choices increasingly define the system’s behavior as much as the model itself.

item.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop…
item.guid: title:spectrag weighted chunk graphs for token budgeted context selection in multi hop
item.description: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation SpectRAG turns your corpus into a weighted chunk graph and uses spectral graph theory to pick evidence that is relevant, diverse and connected. Its index is about 6× smaller than LightRAG’s. 🤹🏼Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) by sourcing external evidence and using that retrieved information to inform generation. While dense retrieval works well for local semantic alignment, standalone ranked retrieval may yield redundant passages, overlook dependencies across chunks, and offer insufficient evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG , a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection !! Ask a RAG system a question for which the answer is spread across three passages and see what happens.

item.title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
item.guid: title:desiderata for the theory of agents
item.description: TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata. A Theory of What? The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time.

item.title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
item.guid: title:kimi k3 open frontier intelligence
item.description: Today, we are introducing Kimi K3 — our most capable model. Kimi K3 is a 2. 8T-parameter model built on our Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals, with native vision capabilities and a 1-million-token context window. It is the world's first open 3T-class model, designed for frontier intelligence across long-horizon coding, knowledge work, and reasoning. While its overall performance still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5. 6 Sol, Kimi K3 demonstrated frontier-level performance across our evaluation suite, consistently outperforming other tested models.

item.title: Learning POMDP World Models from Observations with Language-Model Priors
item.description: arXiv:2605. 13740v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Whether navigating a building, operating a robot, or playing a game, an agent that acts effectively in an environment must first learn an internal model of how that environment works. Partially-observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) provide a flexible modeling class for such internal world models, but learning them from observation-action trajectories alone is challenging and typically requires extensive environment interaction. We ask whether language-model priors can reduce costly interaction by leveraging prior knowledge, and introduce Pinductor (POMDP-inductor): an LLM proposes candidate POMDP models from a few observation-action trajectories and iteratively refines them to optimize a belief-based likelihood score. Despite relying on strictly less information, Pinductor achieves comparable performance and sample efficiency to LLM-based POMDP learning methods with privileged access to hidden states. Moreover, it is up to 330 times more sample-efficient than standard POMDP baselines such as DreamerV3, at comparable computational cost.

item.title: Introducing PerceptionBench
item.guid: title:introducing perceptionbench
item.description: Evaluating Atomic Visual Perception in Multimodal Large Language Models Authors Kimi Team We are releasing PerceptionBench , a benchmark that isolates visual perception and evaluates it as a set of atomic capabilities— discovered from how today's models fail, not defined in advance. From frontier-model failures across 42 benchmarks, we derive 10 atomic perceptual capabilities and construct 3,000 verified questions, each isolating a single capability and answerable by looking, with no reasoning or external knowledge required.
